Six years in, the Xbox Series X still beats the PS5 and Nintendo's Switch 2 where it actually counts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I can already hear the comment section sharpening its pitchforks, so let’s get this out of the way early: yes, I know buying an Xbox in 2026 feels like backing the underdog.

Shopping for a console right now usually comes down to two predictable habits. Most buyers are either chasing Nintendo’s Switch 2 or automatically reaching for a PlayStation 5, a reflex driven by years of internet noise and Microsoft’s own occasionally muddled messaging. Even I fell for the Switch 2’s sturdier Joy-Cons and nicer screen at launch, but soon it was collecting dust.

Once you strip away the badge loyalty and look strictly at how you live with a console day to day, the Xbox Series X makes a strong case as the smartest purchase in gaming. Six years into its run, it has matured into a no-nonsense machine that I’d still pick over the PS5 and Switch 2 for everyday convenience, library value, and big-screen performance.

If you want sprawling RPGs and big-budget releases to look and run their best, the Series X still hits the sweet spot. Yes, I know you can dock the Switch 2 to a TV and it outputs 4K via HDMI, so please save the "well, actually" comments. I just don't enjoy playing massive RPGs on it.

I love my Switch 2 for party games with friends, yet when I want to sink 80 hours into a dense open world, a hybrid console still feels like a compromise next to the Series X’s 4K horsepower and steady frame rates.

Under the hood, the Series X also packs slightly more raw graphical muscle than the standard PS5. In plain English, its graphics processor can crunch more visual data per second (12 teraflops versus the base PS5’s 10.28). While both consoles perform very similarly in most games, that extra power on paper can give the Series X a slight edge in resolution or frame-rate stability in demanding titles without forcing you to pay extra for a PS5 Pro.

Then there’s the elephant in the room, literally. The PS5 is one of the largest home consoles ever made, and personally, I still find it an eyesore. Between the flaring white fins, awkward horizontal stand, and departure from PlayStation's classic all-black, it’s kind of a a nightmare to blend in. The Series X, on the other hand, is a plain, matte-black tower that doesn’t demand to be the centerpiece

Even with subscription prices fluctuating, Microsoft’s ecosystem still stretches my gaming budget further than anything else. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate packs in hundreds of titles alongside day-one releases from Bethesda, Xbox’s own studios, and select Activision games, giving me massive value for what I pay.

My favorite perk, though, is Xbox Cloud Gaming. When I don't fancy clearing hard-drive space for a massive download, streaming games instantly is like sampling ice creams before deciding which one I’m actually sticking on the cone — I’ve even had friends who don't own an Xbox use it to test-drive games before buying them on the PlayStation Store.

Pair that with Xbox Play Anywhere, which gives you both the console and PC version of supported games under a single purchase, and it easily justifies the cost for me.

I have four generations of consoles hooked up in my games room, and nothing beats the quality of life features baked into the Series X.

Quick Resume alone makes going back to a PS5 or Switch 2 feel strangely dated. I’m replaying Red Dead Redemption 2 at the moment, and just holding down the guide button on my controller to wake the TV, clicking the tile, and being dropped straight back into the saddle in seconds completely changes how you game. You can keep three games suspended like this at once.

Add in free cloud saves (which Sony and Nintendo still lock behind paid memberships) and backward compatibility stretching across Series X/S, Xbox One, Xbox 360, and the original Xbox, and the value adds up fast. I can literally play a lifetime's worth of my back catalog on one console.

Buying an Xbox in 2026 doesn't mean sitting out the year’s biggest moments. With GTA 6 arriving on November 19, the Series X gives you day-one access at full current-gen fidelity, something the Switch 2 isn't getting at launch, and even lets Xbox One owners stream it via Cloud Gaming (provided you own the game) while PS4 players are left behind.

People love to dunk on Xbox’s missteps, and putting its games on rival boxes has blurred the old console-war lines. Yet six years in, the Series X runs quiet, its library is stacked, unlike the Switch 2, where you're still betting on future software, and it does what it says on the tin and does it well.

The PS5 may win the popularity contest, the Switch 2 might own party nights, yet, for my money, the Series X remains the best all-rounder console in 2026.

Agree, disagree, or happily sticking with a PC? Let me know in the comments.

#3106. A Larger-Than-Normal Fed Rate Hike in December Now Looks More Likely. Here's Why.

Hotter-than-expected inflation in October means the Fed may raise its target rate by a half percentage point next month.

When it raises interest rates to fight inflation, the Federal Reserve typically moves very gradually, hiking its target rate by a quarter of a percentage point at a time.

But December may be different. That's because, after raising the federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point at its September meeting, the Fed's monetary policy committee paused in October to see if inflation was beginning to cool.

Suddenly, it looks like that was a poor decision. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), the main measure of inflation in the U.S., was just published and showed that inflation was higher than expected in October. The overall price level rose 0.4% month over month, higher than the 0.3% expected and well above the 0.2% level the Fed would like to see.

Higher energy prices, related to the ongoing conflict with Iran, continued to add to overall inflation. But other sectors saw larger-than-expected increases, too, including housing.

As a result, the Fed may have to play catch-up at its last meeting of the year, on Dec. 8-9. That means it could move from its typical quarter-point hike to a half-point hike, which could be jarring for financial markets unused to larger rate increases.

In fact, one Fed official said it out loud. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Nov. 10 in a speech in London that a 50-basis-point (bp) hike -- equivalent to half of a percentage point -- is merited. If October's core CPI rate (the rate that excludes volatile food and fuel costs) came in at 0.3% or higher, he said, "I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting." And indeed, core CPI in October was 0.3%.

Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.

It's not yet clear that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is on board with a 50 bp hike in December, and we may get little indication of how he's leaning before that meeting, as he has come out against giving markets hints of what he's thinking.

But I think he'll be won over to a larger hike. Despite not hiking the federal funds rate in October, Warsh sounded very hawkish at his press conference after the October meeting, and with the economy and the labor market appearing very healthy at the moment, he may reason that a larger rate hike won't harm them much.

Right now, futures traders are pricing in an 87% chance of a quarter-point hike and a 13% chance of a half-point hike. But I believe that will change in the coming weeks. The next key data point to watch is the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, which will be published on Nov. 25.

If that index, like the CPI, comes in hotter than expected, I expect a half-point hike in December.

#3105. Microsoft restores Outlook and Teams after two-day global outage

Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot worldwide, with Claude and ChatGPT integrations also affected

Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York

Microsoft said on Saturday that it had restored service to its remaining customers and regions, about two days after the outage began, the Associated Press reported.

The company said the problem was caused by an issue during an earlier upgrade to its network capacity, which surfaced after a recent network change. It again said there was no sign of malicious activity, and said on Friday that the outage was not caused by AI agents.

Separately, US officials said the outage was not linked to Friday’s nationwide flight ground stop.

A global Microsoft outage has disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services for more than 12 hours, affecting businesses, government agencies, financial institutions and airlines across several continents.

The disruption has also spread to third-party AI services, with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude reporting problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors.

The trouble began on Thursday in the Americas and spread globally within an hour. Outage reports reached 74 countries and territories in that time, according to Downdetector, which recorded a tenfold jump in UK reports at 17:43 UTC, followed by surges in India and New Zealand as their workdays began.

Microsoft has ruled out a cyberattack. Charles Lamanna, the company’s executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X that there was no indication the disruption resulted from malicious or cyber activity.

@MSFT365Status We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue. We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.

— Charles Lamanna (@clamanna) November 13, 2026

However, restoring services has proved more difficult than initially expected. After reporting positive results from its recovery measures, Microsoft said overnight that traffic rerouting and strategic blocking were delivering only partial improvements, rather than sustained recovery.

The company has continued restarting affected servers and applying additional mitigation measures, but some changes have not worked as expected.

The outage has had consequences well beyond Microsoft’s own products. Bankers at Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong told CNN they had been unable to access email and Teams throughout the day.

Japan’s government returned to paper-based processes after ministries struggled to send emails for much of Friday. Australia’s spy agency and federal police were also among the affected organisations.

The Philippine Supreme Court warned of delays, while Australian schools and courts reported email disruptions. US city governments, including Miami Beach and Austin, asked residents to use phone services instead. A Colorado sheriff’s office said the outage had delayed bond payments for prisoners.

Airlines including IndiGo and Akasa lost email support channels, while electric vehicle maker Workhorse postponed its earnings call because of business disruptions. Financial institutions, including Standard Chartered and ING Australia, also warned customers about scammers impersonating technical support staff and attempting to exploit the disruption.

The disruption has extended to AI services that rely on Microsoft’s productivity infrastructure. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors, which allow their AI assistants to access workplace information such as emails, calendars, Teams conversations and SharePoint files.

OpenAI said it was investigating elevated errors affecting its Microsoft 365 connector. The company warned that new connections could fail and that existing tools might not work as expected.

Anthropic reported similar problems with Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector. Mail, calendar and search requests were failing for most users, while some users were also unable to open Claude for Outlook or use its mail and calendar functions.

Anthropic traced the problem to an upstream provider and subsequently confirmed that it was caused by the Microsoft 365 service incident.

The disruption does not mean that ChatGPT or Claude are entirely offline. The problems concern their connections to Microsoft’s services, rather than their underlying AI models. Anthropic’s status page lists the Claude API and Claude Code as operational, although Claude.ai and Claude Cowork have also been reporting degraded performance.

The incidents illustrate how an outage affecting a major productivity platform can spread to third-party applications and AI assistants that depend on its infrastructure.

The likely cause of the disruption remains under investigation. Australia’s home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believed it was dealing with something similar to the CrowdStrike incident in 2024, describing it as an update that had gone wrong, according to CNN.

Microsoft has not confirmed that explanation as the root cause, and its investigation has focused on affected servers and recent configuration changes, while its recovery efforts have centred on restoring capacity and stabilising the infrastructure.

The timing is particularly pointed for Europe, where the outage coincided with EU leaders meeting in Dublin to discuss reducing the continent’s dependence on foreign technology providers.

The 2024 CrowdStrike incident exposed the risks of relying on a small number of technology providers for critical services. The latest Microsoft disruption adds another example of how problems at a single infrastructure provider can affect organisations across industries and countries, including services built by other technology companies.

For businesses relying on Microsoft 365, the incident also raises questions about contingency planning. When email, calendars and workplace collaboration tools become unavailable, organisations can quickly lose access to the systems they depend on to communicate with customers, employees and partners.

As Microsoft’s recovery efforts continue, the outage is a reminder that cloud-based productivity services are interconnected, and that a failure in one part of the ecosystem can have consequences far beyond the company experiencing the technical problem.

#3102. Where Will Micron Stock Be in 5 Years?

Artificial intelligence chatbots and agents are quickly becoming a normal part of many people's everyday lives, and with their growing usage comes the need for much more AI infrastructure to support their needs for compute power.

And that has spurred a further rush to purchase memory chips for data centers, sending Micron Technology's (MU -2.52%) sales and earnings soaring and its share price skyrocketing. It is now up by about 1,010% over the past five years.

What the next five years will look like for Micron stock is difficult to predict. Still, given the company's current position in the memory market and rising demand for memory, its future certainly looks bright. Here's why.

One of the key components of AI infrastructure is memory. The quantity of stored data that processors can rapidly access determines how quickly and at what scale AI systems can train and run models. Data centers rely on several types, notably high bandwidth memory (HBM) and conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM).

Micron isn't the No. 1 provider in either of these niches, but it does hold impressive market shares -- 18% in HBM and 21% in DRAM, according to Counterpoint Research. Those strong positions have allowed Micron to benefit greatly from the booming memory market. In its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 3, revenue rose 380% year over year to $54.2 billion, and non-GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) earnings rose by about 1,000% to $33.42 per share.

Micron has seen boom times similar to these before, and that's what has some investors worried. The memory business has always been highly cyclical, so there's reason to think that memory demand could taper off soon, sending memory prices falling back toward where they were before the current shortage. That would mean Micron would lose the highly favorable gross margin (nearly 81%) that it currently has.

But recent comments from fellow memory giant SK Hynix (SKHY -4.30%) shed some light on just how short on memory tech companies are, and the efforts they are making to try to secure more of it. The company's management said it has already sold through half of its expected memory production for 2027 and 2028.

Even more impressive is that SK Hynix expects the current level of demand to persist through 2030. That's good news for Micron, too, as it shows that tech companies continue to buy as much memory as they can get.

Bank of America estimates technology companies will more than double their AI infrastructure spending by 2028, boosting it to $2 trillion. When you pair that spending boom with this memory shortage, that's a recipe for continued impressive growth from a company with Micron's strong position in both the DRAM and HBM markets.

Investors are trying to guess when the AI boom will end and when the spending spigots will start to close. That's a legitimate concern, but accurately calling the end of any market cycle is nearly impossible, and doing so now, as tech companies are increasing spending, appears illogical.

Most major tech companies have said they plan to further increase their AI spending next year, and research from Deloitte published earlier this year found that the "memory crunch is greater than expected," and might not ease until 2029 at the earliest.

Predicting where a company and its stock will be in five years is no easy task. But Micron has made deals to sell memory through the next several years, and recently said that 26 of its customers have already signed agreements that account for 35% of its expected 2030 production volume. That means we can assume demand will probably remain elevated over the next few years.

Analysts' consensus estimate puts Micron's earnings per share (EPS) at around $201 in 2030. Of course, that is just an estimate, but it represents a 166% increase from fiscal 2026. To get there would take an impressive compound annual growth rate of about 28%. I think that forecast is a little on the aggressive side, and I'd assume a growth rate of half that (closer to 14%) might be a better assumption, putting EPS around $128 in 2030.

Micron trades at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 10 right now, which is far below the technology sector's average P/E ratio of 32. That means you can pick up Micron's shares at a relative bargain price, despite the company being in the midst of the largest growth cycle in its history. Even if it continues to trade at that lower multiple, with EPS of $128, that would give it a share price of $1,280 in 2030. As of Friday morning, Micron was trading at around $762, so that would amount to a 68% gain. And that's based on my conservative earnings projections. If the analysts' consensus is accurate, or the market starts to bestow higher earnings multiples on memory stocks, the gains in the coming years could be considerably greater.

#3101. Italy fines Meta €805m over Facebook’s access to Android photos

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at a dinner with tech leaders in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 4, 2025.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805m, or about $887m. It says the Facebook app for Android accessed photos, videos and their metadata on Italian users’ phones without specific consent or proper notice.

The decision, first reported in English by Reuters, targets a gallery suggestions feature available since 2023. While users scroll Facebook, it offers photos and videos from their phone as ideas for posts.

The Garante found that Facebook asked for gallery access with one permission for the whole app. That request followed a vague prompt to enable other features. Users could not tell they were also switching on gallery suggestions.

The regulator said about 20 million Android users in Italy were affected. It also weighed a 2019 decision against Meta and what it called poor cooperation. Changes Meta made after the complaint counted in its favour, but the Garante called them late and limited to users who update the app.

The fine equals about 0.47% of Meta’s global turnover. Within 60 days, Meta must ask for separate, specific consent for the feature. It must also keep the feature off by default, even for users who already granted access.

The probe did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI, which Meta denies. The Garante will look separately at a cloud processing feature launched in 2026.

The penalty is close to the €825m Dutch fine on Uber, though below Meta’s €1.2bn GDPR fine over data transfers. Meta is also tangling with Italy over a ruling on publisher payments.

Reuters said Meta was not immediately available for comment.

#3100. Tired of paying for cloud storage every month? pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal is the cure for subscription fatigue

Software used to be a one-time purchase, but over time, with the addition of cloud storage and services, everything has become a subscription. One company even tried to make your car seat heaters a subscription. Count the subscriptions you’re paying for right now: iCloud, a password manager, a couple of streaming services, a music service, maybe a VPN, and whatever other app decided this year that it needed to be $4.99 per month for something that used to be a one-time purchase.

Everything is a service now, and a lot of people are hitting the point where one more monthly charge is one too many on principle alone. Cloud storage is the one that’s hardest to cancel, because your photos and files are in it. That’s exactly why pCloud’s Lifetime plans are worth a look this Black Friday: you pay once, and your storage is yours for life!

Apple gives you 5 GB of iCloud for free, which stops being enough about a week after you buy an iPhone. The irony is that they launched with 5 GB of free storage in 2011, and it’s almost laughable that it hasn’t been increased since.

After that, it’s a subscription forever. The 2 TB iCloud+ plan costs $9.99 a month, about $120 a year, for as long as you want your photos to stay where they are. pCloud’s math is different. The 2 TB Lifetime plan is a one-time payment that costs less than four years of iCloud+ at the same size, and the day you buy it is the last day you pay anything for it.

If you’ve been paying for iCloud or Google Drive storage for all of your files for the last 9 years instead of using pCloud, go do the math on how much you’ve spent.

Apple charges a lot to move from a 256 GB MacBook Air to a 512 GB one, and you can’t change your mind later with a hard drive upgrade. Storage has gotten incredibly pricey in recent years as well. pCloud Drive is your solution without breaking the bank. It’s a native Mac app that mounts your pCloud storage as a drive in Finder, so your files appear as if they’re natively on your Mac but live in the cloud until you open them. A 256 GB laptop with a 2 TB pCloud Drive behind it stops feeling small. It runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android, and everything stays in sync across all of them in real time.

With pCloud Backup, backing up the folders you choose is easy and safe from a lost laptop, fire, flood, or theft. If you run a NAS at home, pCloud supports backing it up via WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP, making it a real offsite destination for a Synology NAS, not just a simple sync folder. It would be a perfect offsite backup for small businesses, remote workers, etc.

iCloud Photos is great, but it uses storage from your iCloud storage quota, which can get expensive as Apple’s cameras get better and better and file sizes keep increasing. Every pCloud plan includes pCloud Photos, a photo gallery that organizes everything by date on a timeline, automatically tags objects and scenes, and groups shots into albums by event and person.

The pCloud mobile app backs up your camera roll automatically to free up space on your iPhone; a Memories feature resurfaces older photos, as the Photos app does; and a built-in document scanner turns receipts and paperwork into PDFs without needing a separate app. Inside the app, there is also a built-in Photo Editor with crop, rotate, brightness, contrast, highlights, shadows, and eight one-click filters, so quick fixes don’t require moving it back to Apple Photos.

pCloud Docs covers documents, spreadsheets, presentations, PDFs, text, and markdown with six built-in editors and real-time collaboration, all from the browser or the mobile app. If your household is split, with one person on Microsoft, Apple, or Google, pCloud can pull in files from Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Facebook. That’s the easiest way I’ve seen to get everyone’s files into one place without needing to download and reupload everything.

Files and photos aren’t the only benefit of joining the pCloud ecosystem. pCloud Pass is a password manager that works across all devices, browsers, and operating systems, with one-click login, form filling, and a generator for strong, unique passwords. Passwords are still hard, and most people are either paying monthly for a manager or reusing the same three passwords. A lifetime license solves the annoying aspects of using a dedicated password manager app or being locked into Apple’s or Google’s systems.

pCloud Encryption is client-side, zero-knowledge encryption for your most sensitive files. In plain language: files in your Crypto folder are encrypted on your Mac before they upload, and only you hold the key. pCloud can’t read them, and neither can anyone else. It’s the right place for tax returns, scans of your birth certificate, and anything else you’d rather not have sitting in a regular sync folder.

Here’s the deal you’ll want to pay the most attention to: pCloud offers an exclusive 3in1 Bundle, because it knocks out two more subscriptions at once. It’s 3 TB of Lifetime storage plus Lifetime pCloud Pass and Lifetime pCloud Encryption, and it’s the only offer that includes everything you need to ditch a vast majority of your subscriptions. Count up what this level of storage and functionality would cost you over three or four years, and you’ll see how incredible of a deal it is. If you don’t sign up today, you’ll end up regretting it in 2030.

pCloud’s Black Friday pricing runs from November 13 through November 28. Every plan is a one-time payment with Lifetime access, no subscription, and no renewal.

You also get to choose where your data is stored, with data centers in Luxembourg and the United States, and everything is protected in transit with TLS/SSL. With pCloud, it’s your files and your rules, and one Lifetime deal protects everything.

If you’re tired of paying for storage every month, this is the week to stop. Grab pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal before it ends on November 28.

The best time to sign up for pCloud’s lifetime deal was 9 years ago. The second best is today.

Garmin’s top adventure watches have different strengths

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Fenix 9 Pro is Garmin's flagship watch and offers a more attractive design than the Enduro 4, along with extra features and more choice in the size and display you get.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is cheaper and lighter than the Fenix 9 Pro, and offers better battery life too.

Buying one of the best Garmin watches brings with it some guarantees with regard to the features you can expect, especially at the higher end of the brand’s line-up, where the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Garmin Enduro 4 both sit.

These watches offer stellar sports tracking and training analysis, along with the best navigation tools you’ll find on a smartwatch thanks to their offline routable maps. They are also equally accurate with GPS and heart rate, in my experience, and run the same software.

However, after testing the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Enduro 4 extensively, there are certainly some key differences between the two in other areas, most notably design and battery life.

If you want more details on either watch, check out my Garmin Fenix 9 Pro review or Garmin Enduro 4 review, but read on for a summary of the differences between them I noticed when testing them individually and at the same time.

The biggest difference between the two watches is price, since the Garmin Enduro 4 costs much less than the Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll pay $899 for the Enduro 4 right now, while the cheapest Fenix 9 Pro model is $1,099, whether you choose the AMOLED version or the Fenix 9 Pro Solar with a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display like the Enduro.

The key thing that the Fenix 9 Pro offers with its design is choice. It comes in three sizes — 43mm, 47mm and 51mm — and you can pick between an AMOLED or MIP display, and even choose between colors for the bezel and sensor guard.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In contrast, the Enduro 4 comes in one style and size. It’s a 51mm watch with a MIP display, and it only uses titanium for its bezel, with a mostly plastic case, whereas the Fenix 9 Pro has a full titanium case.

This gives the Fenix 9 Pro a more elegant look, but it also makes it considerably heavier than the Enduro 4. I tested a 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED, and both it and the Enduro 4 are large watches, but the Enduro 4 counters that a little by being so light.

When it comes to the display, picking between AMOLED and MIP will come down to personal preferences.

I find AMOLED brighter and clearer in almost all conditions, and just as good as MIP in bright sunlight these days, and I prefer using an AMOLED watch in general, but MIP uses less power and is less obvious on the wrist, and the Enduro 4’s display was still clear enough to see at all times.

Both watches have sapphire crystal screens and built-in flashlights, but you get an extra green mode on the Fenix 9 Pro’s flashlight.

You also get a diveproof watch with the Fenix 9 Pro, which can be used to depths of 40m. The Enduro 4 has a high waterproof rating of 10ATM and is fine for swimming, but isn’t a diving watch.

Another addition on the Fenix line is a mic and speaker, which can be used to take voice notes and give voice commands to the watch.

One advantage of the Enduro 4 is that it ships with Garmin's fabric ComfortFit band as standard, which I much prefer to the silicone band on the Fenix 9 Pro. You can buy the ComfortFit band separately, but it will cost $59.

The design differences speak to the approach behind the two watches. The Enduro 4 is built to be simpler and lighter, which helps it to be more affordable, but the Fenix 9 Pro is the all-singing, all-dancing option with a variety of models to pick between.

The two watches share very similar sports tracking and training analysis features, and both have proved to be similarly accurate throughout my testing.

There’s only one difference worth flagging in this area, which is that the Fenix 9 Pro is a diveproof watch and has Garmin’s scuba, apnea and snorkel sports modes.

One of the biggest features you get on the Fenix 9 Pro (InReach model) that isn’t available on the Enduro 4 is LTE and satellite connectivity.

This feature requires a subscription but allows you to stay in contact with the world when you’re off the grid or phone-free, through messaging and the ability to send SOS alerts.

Otherwise, both watches share the usual Garmin smart features. They can store music and link to streaming services, make NFC payments through Garmin Pay, and have access to the Connect IQ app store.

Along with being cheaper and lighter, the main advantage of the Enduro 4 is its incredible battery life.

Whatever Fenix 9 Pro you opt for, including the Solar MIP watch, the Enduro 4 will outlast it in both watch and GPS modes, partly because it has a bigger solar ring than the Fenix 9 Pro Solar.

I've compared the 51mm models of the Fenix 9 Pro to the Enduro 4 below. Note that to get the full solar battery life listed, you need to be out and about in sunny conditions for three hours a day on average.

In my use, the Enduro 4 lasted me 16 days on its first charge and is tracking for 17-18 on its second charge, whereas the 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED lasts me 10-11 days with the screen set to always-on.

This was during the British winter too, when I gave the Enduro 4 almost nothing in terms of a solar charging boost, so you can expect the gap to be wider in sunnier climates.

13.3mm (43mm),13.8mm (47mm), 15.8mm (51mm)

10 days (43 mm), 18 days (47mm), 31 days (51mm) (raise to wake)

18 hours (43mm), 32 hours (47mm), 56 hours (51mm)

The Garmin Fenix 9 Pro line-up offers more features and choice than the Enduro 4, and I prefer the all-titanium design of the Fenix and its brighter AMOLED display.

However, the Enduro 4’s relative simplicity will appeal to many people, as will its lower price, longer battery life, and lighter design.

If you’ve been eyeing the Fenix 9 Pro Solar in particular and don’t really need the connectivity features on the watch, then I think the Enduro 4 is a better value buy. Or even the Garmin Enduro 3, for that matter, since it has a similar design and feature set to the latest model.

#3097. Jensen Huang struggled to reach Beijing’s chip policymakers, FT says

Nvidia had no dedicated China government team until late 2025, and Beijing’s security camp won the argument over its chips.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang during his GTC 2026 keynote at the SAP Center in San Jose, 16 March 2026

Jensen Huang spent years courting China, but he struggled to reach the officials who decided Nvidia’s fate there, the Financial Times reported. The paper cited people familiar with the matter.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. He had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Beijing denies she is a spy, and the two are not related.

The FT looks at what came before. Huang visited China six times in three years. His first recorded meeting with a top leader came in April 2025, with Vice-Premier He Lifeng. In July 2025 he met He again, and commerce minister Wang Wentao too.

Those meetings ran through Ren Hongbin, who heads China’s main trade promotion body, the FT said. But Nvidia never secured talks with the National Development and Reform Commission. The FT says the state planner led Beijing’s push to restrict Nvidia chips.

Huang also failed to win more time with Wang once those curbs arrived. Part of the problem was Nvidia’s thin lobbying, the FT said. It had no dedicated team for Chinese officials until late 2025, when it hired Tony Jiang from Intel.

Beijing was also split, according to the paper. The commerce ministry saw Nvidia chips as a bridge while Huawei caught up. Security officials saw reliance on Nvidia as a weakness, and their view has gained ground over the past year.

Huang often warned Washington that export curbs would only help Huawei. Now some say his exit will do the same.

“It may sound ironic, but the fall of Jensen helps to strengthen Huawei’s leading position in China,” George Chen, a partner at the Asia Group, told the FT.

In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump’s business delegation to China. He briefly spoke with Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang, the most senior leaders he had met in public.

Nvidia, the commerce ministry and China’s cyberspace regulator did not respond to the FT. Nvidia’s board inquiry continues, and it reports third-quarter results on 17 November.

#3096. Credo Technology Group vs. Marvell Technology: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Credo's revenue surged past 160% in the latest twelve months, but Marvell's $9.5 billion scale and heavier debt load tell a very different story for investors.

As demand for artificial intelligence continues to reshape the global data landscape, investors are weighing the explosive growth of Credo Technology Group (CRDO -5.94%) against the established dominance of Marvell Technology (MRVL -4.68%).

Credo specializes in energy-efficient connectivity for high-speed networks, focusing on specific bottlenecks in hyperscale data centers. Marvell offers a more diverse range of semiconductor solutions covering storage, optical, and computing needs across the entire networking ecosystem. Comparing these two reveals a choice between a high-growth specialist and a diversified infrastructure giant.

Credo focuses on designing high-speed copper and optical interconnect solutions that facilitate massive data movements within cloud networks. The company primarily serves blue chip hyperscalers and equipment manufacturers, with high-profile partnerships including Oracle (ORCL -1.39%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.17%). Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as nearly 90% of revenue in its latest annual report came from just 10 customers.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached close to $1.6 billion, representing explosive growth of approximately 165.1% compared to the prior period. This rapid scaling helped the company generate a net income of roughly $538.3 million during that time frame. The resulting net margin of 33.8% highlights how effectively the company is translating its semiconductor stock sales into actual earnings as it expands.

As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures whether a company can cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, is 10.2x. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, indicating a balance sheet with no total debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended May 2, 2026, free cash flow was approximately $407.0 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 39.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow in the cash flow statement.

Marvell Technology provides the foundational hardware required to move, store, and process data across cloud and automotive markets. The company has a strong focus on the data center segment, which is increasingly driven by demand for custom silicon and high-speed networking. Marvell also maintains high customer concentration, as its top 10 customers accounted for roughly 82% of its revenue in its latest annual report.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue was nearly $9.5 billion, representing revenue growth of approximately 30.6%. The company reported a net income of nearly $2.6 billion, which translates to a healthy net margin of 27.9%. While its growth is slower than its smaller rival, the sheer scale of its operations provides a broader footprint across the enterprise networking and carrier infrastructure industries.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, Marvell has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.3x, meaning it has roughly $0.30 in total debt per dollar of shareholder equity. Its current ratio is 2.0x, suggesting it maintains a comfortable buffer to meet its short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow in the cash flow statement.

Credo Technology Group faces significant revenue concentration risk due to its reliance on a small group of large customers that issue purchase orders rather than long-term commitments. The company faces intense competition from established giants like Broadcom (AVGO -4.76%) and newer entrants like Astera Labs (ALAB -2.62%). Geopolitical tensions between Taiwan and mainland China also pose supply chain vulnerabilities, while the cyclical nature of the chip market could lead to volatility in demand for high-speed connectivity products.

Marvell Technology faces substantial risks from customer concentration and the constant pressure to win design slots with major cloud providers. The company is managing a complex integration of its proposed $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum, which could strain financial resources if expected synergies do not materialize. Marvell also navigates a competitive landscape where large technology firms are increasingly designing their own custom chips, potentially reducing the total addressable market for third-party semiconductor providers.

Credo appears more attractive on a price-to-earnings basis, while Marvell trades at a slightly lower multiple relative to its trailing 12-month sales.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

When comparing Credo and Marvell, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.

Firstly, we should consider revenue growth. Both companies are delivering fantastic growth, but Credo can claim an advantage in the category. It has delivered average year-over-year revenue growth of 143% over the last three years. Marvell, meanwhile, has averaged 24% revenue growth.

Another factor to consider is each company's profitability. Again, Credo has an edge. Its operating margin stands at 32%, while Marvell's is 17%. That said, both companies have been consistently profitable for more than a year.

Finally, there's valuation. Given their profitability, we can examine each company's price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple. Once again, Credo comes out on top. Its 47x P/E multiple is ever so slightly more affordable than Marvell's 52x multiple.

To sum up, growth-oriented investors may want to consider both of these tech stocks. They both exhibit fantastic growth and solid profitability. That said, for me, Credo wins the head-to-head matchup given its stellar growth, better profitability, and more modest valuation.

#3095. Apple @ Work: The spiritual successor to the Xserve is here, thanks to Apple silicon and MLX

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI. Two things happened that make me think Apple knew that all along (or maybe they didn’t and got lucky). Meta released its most capable open-weight model yet and optimized it to run on a Mac Studio. I also spent time with Osaurus, an app that runs a usable local AI model on something as small as a 16 GB Apple silicon laptop without needing a network connection. They even have two models that will run on 8 GB.

The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For the last few years, the narrative has been that Apple fell behind in AI because it didn’t have a frontier model. Siri AI got delayed, and the Apple Intelligence rollout was not great. In hindsight, I think Apple was right not to run that race, as the frontier-model business has turned into somewhat of a capital bonfire. Every frontier lab is spending billions on GPUs to be the best for a few months at a time, and the moment a model is good enough, someone else releases an open-weight version that runs on hardware you already own.

Open-weight models prove it: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active parameters, and a million-token context window, and Meta is giving it away. Apple didn’t build that LLM. It built the hardware that runs it. With that being said, Siri is still far behind.

Look at what Apple has shipped while everyone was waiting on them to try to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI. With Apple silicon’s unified memory, the GPU can use up to 512 GB of memory on a single Mac Studio, instead of being limited to whatever fits on a graphics card.

MLX is Apple’s machine learning framework, and it’s built specifically for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon. If you’ve used NumPy, the API will feel familiar right away. On top of that, MLX includes higher-level packages for neural networks and optimizers, along with function transformations for automatic differentiation and graph optimization, so you can build more complex models without giving up efficiency. It also has bindings in Swift, C++, and C, which means it runs on any Apple platform.

Apple’s own Machine Learning Research post shows four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open at over 36 tokens per second, which is faster than you can read, while peaking around 300 watts per machine.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

That’s the Xserve pitch, rebuilt for 2026. Apple killed the Xserve in 2011 because nobody wanted a Mac in a data center. The Mac mini came along and provided some new use cases over the years. Now, a couple of Mac Studios can host a model that would otherwise require a rack of Nvidia hardware and a power budget to match, and it does so quietly enough to sit under a desk. Apple wasn’t trying to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Nvidia. It was building the infrastructure for everything except the frontier model, and it looks like that’s where the market is going. A company like MacStadium has to be loving this future as well.

The Mac Studio story is the headline, but what matters most to most IT teams is at the other end of the lineup. I had Terence Pae, co-founder and CEO of Osaurus, on the Apple @ Work podcast last week. Osaurus is a free, open-source AI tool for the Mac. It helps manage local models that work offline, but it can also call a frontier model when needed. A really cool feature, when it does this, is that Osaurus runs a small local model first to find names, phone numbers, and account numbers in whatever you pasted, and swaps them for placeholders before anything goes to Claude or OpenAI.

Osaurus has no servers and no customer database. If the company went out of business tomorrow, the app would keep running until macOS broke it. Individuals use it for free. Workspaces, the paid tier, is for teams who want to share agents across their own Macs. There’s a Windows beta as well, which I think helps Apple’s case more than it hurts it. When the same app runs on both platforms, the Mac’s unified memory is the difference.

In talking with him, Terence mentioned he wouldn’t be surprised if a local model matches what today’s frontier models can do by this time next year. I believe him, and that’s the point. The frontier will keep moving, but good enough keeps moving too, and good enough is what most employees need most of the day. Apple spent the AI race building memory, bandwidth, and a framework instead of trying to match the frontier, and the narrative was that they were behind.

Now the most capable open-weight model in the US is optimized for the Mac.

Fall is in full swing, and if your yard looks anything like mine, you’re probably busy clearing scattered leaves while tending to a tired lawn.

What makes it look so worn down are probably the sparse, empty spots across the yard — which leaves me asking: is it too late to plant grass seed in November?

Luckily, I called on some lawn experts to shed some light on this and offer their advice on achieving a lush, resilient lawn even in this colder season.

So before you get ready to sow, here is what you need to consider before grabbing your seed packet and getting started.

While November is typically not the right month to sow grass seed, this can also depend on your regional climate, local soil temperatures, and grass seed type.

For instance, with cool-season grasses (such as Kentucky bluegrass, perennial ryegrass, tall fescue), you should only overseed once the temperatures drop below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

“It’s not necessarily too late — but it is more of a riskier time to do so,” advises Chris Bonnett, founder of GardeningExpress. “If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like where you are.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

“The soil temperature is the most important thing, as the seeds will need a mild environment to germinate, and you'll need the soil temperatures to be consistently around 46.4 °F to 50 °F or above for germination.”

"If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like"

On the other hand, warm-season varieties like Bermuda grass, zoysiagrass, centipedegrass, and Bahiagrass begin going dormant as the weather cools down. As a result, planting them during cold spells reduces their chances of growing. This is especially the case during colder snaps and the risk of frost.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost, so it has time to germinate and build some root growth before winter dormancy sets in," advises Matthew Koch, Ph.D., research and development at ScottsMiracle-Gro.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost

"Regions that experience a milder fall, also known as the Transition Zone (roughly Kansas through the Mid-Atlantic, including areas extending toward the Carolinas), might be able to have one final feeding before winter, but it is entirely dependent on the local climate, growing conditions, and grass type."

However, if the soil is too cold, experts suggest waiting until warmer weather begins during springtime. “I’d recommend waiting until the spring, adds Bonnett.

"There’s no benefit in rushing to sow grass seed if it’s not going to have the right conditions to germinate and establish well.”

So if temperatures haven’t yet dropped, what is the best method for overseeding a lawn? To give your lawn an optimal head start in establishing healthy grass, experts suggest sowing a fast-germinating seed mix.

“If the conditions are mild enough, choose a fast-germinating grass seed mix such as one containing perennial ryegrass,” adds Bonnett. “This will help give your lawn the best chance of establishing.”

Of course, preparation is essential, so start by eliminating weeds, clearing leaves, and leveling the ground with a rake before you start seeding.

“Scatter the seed evenly and gently rake it into the top layer of the soil. Keep the area slightly moist but avoid overwatering, especially in November when rainfall is more frequent. If the ground is already wet or waterlogged, avoid planting.”

For more top tips, check out how to overseed your lawn in fall for the best results in spring.

#3093. Warren Buffett's Berkshire Compounded at More Than 19% a Year Over Six Decades, Nearly Double the S&P 500's 10% Return. Can Investors Still Apply That Playbook Today?

Warren Buffett is widely considered to be the greatest investor of all time. That's not an official title, but there is tangible data supporting the Oracle of Omaha's stellar reputation. As the head of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.47%) (BRKB +0.53%), Buffett delivered average annual returns of more than 19% over six decades. It's hard enough to beat the market over a single 10-year period. Doing it for 60 years is extraordinary. But can investors still apply Buffett's principles in today's market? Let's find out.

Buffett's investing strategy sounds simple on the surface. It boils down to buying shares in companies with strong moats at attractive prices and holding onto them for a long time. However, there is a lot more hiding under the hood. And we can glean important lessons from certain details.

For instance, Warren Buffett has historically avoided certain sectors, including technology. That doesn't mean Berkshire Hathaway has never invested in any tech company. But Buffett himself focuses primarily on relatively simple businesses he understands well, that generate steady cash flows, and have business models that remain more or less unchanged over the long run.

This is an important aspect of the Oracle of Omaha's investing philosophy. The easier it is to forecast a company's future cash flows, the easier it tends to be to determine when it is trading at an attractive price, since, according to one school of investing, a business' intrinsic value is just the value of all of its future cash flows discounted at an appropriate rate.

Buffett's long-term mindset is another important aspect of his strategy. It's always difficult to predict a stock's short-term movement, but as Benjamin Graham, Buffett's mentor, once said: "In the short run, the stock market is a voting machine. But in the long run, it is a weighing machine." Since value drives long-term performance, short-term volatility is no reason to panic-sell.

Staying put over the long run also grants investors tax advantages while putting the magic of compounding to good use, especially with dividend stocks. This isn't quite all there is to Buffett's strategy. But it's a good start.

Emulating Buffett isn't easy. Investors certainly shouldn't expect returns similar to those of the Oracle of Omaha. If it were easy to pull that off, any number of Wall Street hedge fund managers would, but in fact, many of them fail to do so. Warren Buffett once bet $1 million that a low-cost index fund would outperform a group of hedge funds over a decade.

Buffett won the bet hands down, and that's another important lesson we can take from the man's philosophy. For many investors, it's best to simply buy low-cost index funds that track major indexes. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.38%) is a good option in that vein. It has a low expense ratio of just 0.03% and closely tracks the performance of the S&P 500.

This approach is superior for many people. Index funds can offer excellent long-term returns with minimal fees and time spent doing research. But for investors who insist on picking individual stocks, Buffett's approach can also work. Investing in businesses you know and understand well is an important first step.

Making sure the company in question has a moat that allows it to maintain a solid position in its market over the long run is another key box to check. Next, always remember that valuation matters. Even an excellent company with a wide moat can underperform broader equities for investors who purchase its shares at the wrong time. Finally, it's important to stay the course.

That includes keeping your position intact -- or adding shares -- amid a bear market, and selling only when certain conditions are met, such as a material change in the business' outlook. Investors who apply this playbook can beat the market over long periods, although perhaps not to the extent that Buffett has.

#3092. How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program offers ethics and compliance training

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

#3091. Here’s a HomeView feature that should come to every Apple device

This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

On iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

What to remember about Annabeth, Thalia Grace, Kronos and more

There’s not long to wait until Percy Jackson returns for another mythological adventure, with season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” arriving on Disney+ on November 20. Based on Rick Riordan’s third novel, the new instalment sees Walker Scobell’s Percy embark on a dangerous quest after Annabeth Chase (Leah Sava Jeffries) is captured by the forces of Kronos.

With Grover (Aryan Simhadri) by his side, Percy must rescue his friend, free a goddess in chains and confront a prophecy that could spell disaster for Olympus. There are plenty of familiar faces returning, alongside exciting newcomers including Nico and Bianca di Angelo, while Thalia Grace (Tamara Smart) looks set to play an increasingly important role. But before we dive back into Camp Half-Blood, here are five things worth remembering from the first two seasons.

Fair warning: I’ll be spoiling major events from seasons 1 and 2. So, without further ado, here are five things you should remember before “Percy Jackson” season 3.

Thalia Grace’s return at the end of season 2 comes with a major twist that changes everything heading into season 3. In the original books, Zeus turned his daughter into a pine tree to save her life after monsters mortally wounded her. However, the series reveals that he actually imprisoned her as punishment after she refused to obey him and become his weapon in the coming war.

When Clarisse (Dior Goodjohn) uses the Golden Fleece to heal Camp Half-Blood’s protective borders, Thalia returns to human form. The revelation also raises questions about who the demigods can trust. Chiron (Glynn Turman) and the camp’s leaders had hidden the truth about Thalia from Percy, Annabeth and Grover for years. Her hatred of Zeus could also bring her closer to Luke Castellan (Charlie Bushnell) and Kronos, although where her loyalties ultimately lie remains unclear.

Most importantly, Thalia’s return complicates the Great Prophecy. As Zeus’s daughter, she’s another child of the Big Three who could fulfil the prediction, meaning Percy might not be the only demigod capable of deciding Olympus’s fate.

Thalia’s return wasn’t just a side effect of healing Camp Half-Blood. It also gave Kronos another way to threaten Olympus. The Great Prophecy states that a child of one of the “Big Three” gods (Zeus, Poseidon or Hades) who reaches the age of 16 will decide whether Olympus survives or falls.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Before Thalia returned, Percy was the main demigod connected to the prophecy. Now, Zeus’s daughter could also fulfil it, making the situation much more complicated. The two immediately clash after Thalia wakes up, setting up a potential rivalry between them.

Her return also gives Kronos another opportunity to turn a powerful demigod against the gods. Thalia has plenty of reasons to hate Zeus, which could make her vulnerable to his influence. As season 3 approaches, both Percy and Thalia could play a major role in deciding the fate of Olympus.

After the battle at Thalia’s tree, Percy briefly sees his father, Poseidon (Toby Stephens), in a vision while unconscious. Poseidon tells him that the war against Kronos has officially begun and asks Percy’s Cyclops half-brother, Tyson (Daniel Diemer), to help make weapons in the underwater forges.

Tyson happily accepts, finally feeling like he has a place alongside his father. However, his departure leaves Percy facing the growing threat on his own. While Tyson gets a chance to help the gods prepare for war, Percy must return to Camp Half-Blood and deal with the dangers ahead.

The moment also shows that the conflict with Kronos is much bigger than the fight at camp. With Tyson helping build weapons beneath the sea, season 3 could explore more of the underwater world and Poseidon’s role in the coming war.

Luke Castellan has become an increasingly dangerous threat by the end of season 2. Although Clarisse successfully retrieves the Golden Fleece for Camp Half-Blood, Luke’s forces still achieve something important: Thalia is brought back to life, giving Kronos another powerful demigod who could join his side.

The attack also exposes how poorly Camp Half-Blood is being run. After King Tantalus (Timothy Simons) is killed during the siege, Dionysus (Jason Mantzoukas) reluctantly takes charge again but does little to organize the campers. Instead, Percy steps up and gives an inspiring speech, encouraging everyone to defend their home.

This also helps explain why Luke has turned against the Olympian gods. He believes they mistreat their children and care more about their own power than the demigods’ lives. With Zeus’s treatment of Thalia only adding to that argument, Luke has plenty of ammunition to convince others to join Kronos. Heading into season 3, he’s still a major threat to Percy and everyone at Camp Half-Blood.

Season 3 adapts “The Titan’s Curse,” which sees Annabeth Chase captured by Kronos’ forces. Her disappearance sets Percy on another dangerous quest to rescue his friend, but it also puts his biggest weakness to the test: his loyalty to the people he loves.

Percy has always been willing to put himself in danger to protect his friends, even when it means ignoring warnings or going against the gods. With Annabeth’s life at stake, that side of him is likely to become even more important in season 3.

The trailer also shows Percy carrying the weight of the sky, a burden traditionally associated with the Titan Atlas. It’s another example of how far he’s willing to go to protect the people closest to him. As the Great Prophecy draws closer, Percy will have to balance his feelings for Annabeth and his friends with the fate of Olympus.

"Percy Jackson and the Olympians" season 3 premieres with two episodes on Disney Plus on November 20. After that, new episodes arrive weekly on Fridays.

#3089. Alibaba vs. Uber Technologies: Which Tech Platform Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Alibaba and Uber both lead their markets, but one trades at a far lower earnings multiple while the other is priced for sustained high growth.

Global platforms like Alibaba Group (BABA +0.02%) and Uber Technologies (UBER +0.83%) dominate their respective markets through massive scale. Choosing between these giants requires weighing deep value in Asia against high-growth mobility services.

Alibaba operates at the heart of the Chinese digital economy, while Uber connects the physical world through rides and logistics. While both rely on network effects to maintain their leads, they face different regulatory landscapes and geographic drivers. This comparison examines their financials and risks to help you decide which stock is the better buy.

Alibaba is a global technology leader focused on cloud computing and commerce. The company operates massive marketplaces in China, such as Taobao and Tmall, which are core components of the broader consumer discretionary stocks market. Its strategy centers on integrating artificial intelligence into its cloud infrastructure to serve enterprises while expanding its international digital commerce operations in Southeast Asia and Europe.

In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, revenue reached around $153.7 billion, representing growth of approximately 2.7% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company reported net income of about $15.6 billion for this period, although this was a decrease from the year before. This trend reflects a competitive retail environment in China and significant investments in new technology initiatives and international market expansion.

As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.2x. This ratio divides total debt by shareholder equity to show how much a company relies on borrowing. The current ratio stands at approximately 1.3x, which measures the ability to cover short-term obligations by comparing current assets to current liabilities. According to the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 report, free cash flow was a negative $7.6 billion, representing cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

Uber Technologies operates a massive technology platform connecting riders with drivers and consumers with merchants. The company relies on significant commercial partnerships, including work with McDonald's (MCD -0.61%) for global delivery and Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN -0.29%) to provide services for Prime members. Uber also maintains a critical mapping partnership with Alphabet (GOOGL -0.98%) to ensure its platform remains functional for millions of monthly users worldwide.

In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached approximately $52.0 billion, which was an increase of more than 18% over the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $10.1 billion, continuing a trend of improved profitability following years of heavy losses. This growth was driven by increased demand for mobility services and a maturing food delivery business that has become a staple for urban consumers.

According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is nearly 0.4x. This metric helps investors understand the company's financial leverage by comparing its total debt to the value of its equity. The current ratio is approximately 1.1x, indicating that the company has slightly more current assets than liabilities due within one year. Free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, was about $9.8 billion, which is the cash remaining after subtracting capital expenditures from operating cash flow.

Alibaba faces substantial risks related to the regulatory environment in China and ongoing geopolitical tensions. Changes in government policy can abruptly affect its domestic e-commerce operations or its cloud computing business. Additionally, the company faces intense competition from local rivals such as PDD Holdings (PDD +1.86%) and JD.com (JD +1.53%), which put pressure on its net margin. Any slowdown in Chinese consumer spending also directly impacts its core revenue streams.

Uber Technologies is subject to significant legal and regulatory risks, particularly concerning the classification of drivers as independent contractors rather than employees. A shift in these regulations could materially increase operating costs and force changes to its business model. The company also competes in a crowded market against Lyft (LYFT +2.23%) and DoorDash (DASH -0.62%), which limits its ability to raise prices. Furthermore, it faces potential liabilities from ongoing litigation regarding safety incidents on its platform.

Alibaba trades at a significantly lower earnings multiple than Uber, suggesting it is the value play while Uber is priced for continued high growth.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Uber revolutionized the taxi industry when it rolled out its ride-sharing network, allowing anyone with a car to earn a side gig. Both the industry and the companies have come a long way.

Uber Technologies is by far the largest player in the developing ride-share market in terms of revenue. Wall Street expects Uber's sales to increase $6 billion from last year to $58 billion this year, bringing with it net income of $6.4 billion. But as a sign of the expenses Uber faces in expanding its business model, that would be roughly $3.6 billion less income than in 2025. In the long run, its global ride-sharing, delivery, and autonomous solutions business will make for a strong business.

Alibaba focuses on defending its cash-rich China e-commerce marketplaces, Taobao and Tmall, while funneling capital into higher-growth AI cloud and AI services. Alibaba is the public cloud leader in China and the owner of the Qwen open- and closed-source models. Yet its retail businesses are losing market share to Chinese rivals, which crimps the business's ability to fund money-losing AI model efforts. That means its AI cloud and compute services are the one impressive growth center for the business. It grew 45% year over year in that sector. One metric in its favor is that the current valuation of Alibaba is attractive relative to U.S. cloud and AI peers.

Alibaba is forecast to continue growing, but some one the Street are skeptical of the company's ability to win in the hyper-competitive Chinese market and to expand its fast-growing AI services business beyond the China-dominated region, especially given the capital investment needed for AI.

BABA looks like a value play, but UBER is hardly priced at a premium, trading just over the average forward P/E of the S&P 500. Buying Uber Technologies at current levels makes for a better buy in 2027, given the volatility of AI and the Chinese consumer.
